front: Who held that a moving body needs something external to keep it moving?
back: Aristotle (384–322 B.C.). The fallacy: he coded the ever-present effect of friction into a false 'law'.

front: What was Galileo's key conclusion about uniform linear motion?
back: The state of rest and the state of uniform linear motion are equivalent — both need no net force. With no friction, a ball on a horizontal plane moves forever.

front: State Newton's first law of motion.
back: Every body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by an external force. Equivalently: zero net external force ⟹ zero acceleration.

front: How can we infer the presence of forces from uniform motion?
back: If an object on Earth is at rest or in uniform motion, the net external force must be zero — the various forces exactly cancel.

front: Define momentum and give F = ma via momentum.
back: Momentum p = mv (Eq. 4.1). The second law: F = dp/dt = ma, with k = 1, so 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

front: What does it mean that the second law is a vector law?
back: It holds component-wise: Fₓ = maₓ, F_y = ma_y, F_z = ma_z. A force changes only the velocity component parallel to itself.

front: What is impulse? When is it useful?
back: Impulse = FΔt = Δp — the change in momentum. It is measurable even when a huge force acts over a tiny, unmeasurable time (ex: a bat hitting a ball).

front: State the impulse–momentum result for a ball reversing direction at speed u mass m.
back: Δp = 2mu perpendicular to the wall if the hit is normal; general case: change in the component of momentum normal to the wall.

front: State Newton's third law clearly.
back: F_AB = −F_BA. Forces always occur in pairs, act simultaneously on DIFFERENT bodies, equal and opposite; there is no cause–effect order.

front: Why can't you add 'action' and 'reaction' and get zero net force?
back: They act on different bodies. They only cancel when the two bodies are treated as ONE system, where the pair becomes internal.

front: State the law of conservation of momentum.
back: For an isolated system, p_A' + p_B' = p_A + p_B. Mutual forces cancel in pairs; holds for both elastic and inelastic collisions.

front: When is a particle in equilibrium?
back: When the net external force on it is zero: then it is at rest or in uniform motion. For three forces, F₁ + F₂ + F₃ = 0 (closed force triangle).

front: What are the two components of a contact force?
back: The normal reaction (perpendicular to the surfaces) and friction (parallel to them). Contact forces are ultimately electrical in origin.

front: What is static friction's key property?
back: It is self-adjusting: fₛ ≤ (fₛ)ₘₐₓ = μₛN, opposing IMPENDING motion, independent of the contact area.

front: How does kinetic friction differ from static friction?
back: f_k = μₖN once sliding starts, with μₖ < μₛ; fₖ is roughly independent of area and speed. The relations are empirical, not fundamental.

front: Why is no friction needed for ideal rolling?
back: The point of contact is momentarily at rest (no slipping). Real rolling friction is tiny — 2–3 orders of magnitude smaller than sliding friction.

front: Where does the centripetal force come from on a level road turn?
back: Static friction alone: mv²/R ≤ fₛₘₐₓ = μₛmg, giving vₘₐₓ = √(μₛRg) — independent of the car's mass.

front: What is the optimum speed on a banked road?
back: v₀ = (Rg tanθ)^½ — needs no friction; below it friction acts up the slope (parking demands tanθ ≤ μₛ).

front: How do you draw a free-body diagram?
back: Draw the chosen system alone (not pals/support plus environment), include EVERY force on it (weight, normal, friction, tension, etc.), omit forces the system exerts on the environment, then apply the laws of motion.

front: Is the weight mg of a body an action–reaction pair with the normal force R?
back: No. They act on the SAME body. (Equal-and-opposite forces on one body are never a 3rd-law pair.) Pairs act on two different bodies — e.g. block-on-floor and floor-on-block.

front: Mass of 0.05 kg thrown vertically up, g = 10: net force during upward motion? At the top?
back: 0.5 N downward in both — weight is always mg downward; at the top the velocity is zero but the force and acceleration are still g downward.

front: A stone is released from an accelerating train window; what is the net force on it just after release?
back: Just mg = 1 N downward (mass 0.1 kg). Force is a local, instantaneous concept — no memory of the train's motion imparts a horizontal force.

front: Why does the gun recoil when fired?
back: Time-symmetric, body-wise view: by the 3rd law the gun feels −F on the bullet; same contact time Δt ⟹ momentum gained by gun equals that given to bullet, the total staying zero.
